# How does Postgres MVCC work? Cover xmin/xmax, vacuum, and the relationship to long-running transactions.

*Generated by Blitz-Swarm on 2026-11-04 23:51*

### Scope and evidence

This completes the missing VACUUM, autovacuum, and transaction-ID sections and clarifies how transaction lifetime affects cleanup. It targets PostgreSQL 17. Sources are primary documentation by the PostgreSQL Global Development Group (2024); links and details are recalled from knowledge and were not checked live, as instructed. Configuration numbers below are documented defaults or implementation limits, not experimentally measured performance results. No universal bloat rate or performance penalty is claimed.

### MVCC: why obsolete row versions remain

PostgreSQL generally implements an UPDATE by creating a new heap tuple version and marking the old version as superseded. A tuple's `xmin` identifies its inserting transaction. Its `xmax` can identify a deleting or updating transaction, but can also encode locking information, including a MultiXact. Therefore, a nonzero `xmax` does not by itself establish that a tuple is deleted: transaction status and tuple-header flags also matter. [PGDG, 2024, System Columns](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/ddl-system-columns.html), [Database Page Layout](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/storage-page-layout.html).

Snapshot visibility depends on which transactions had committed when the snapshot was established, including which were still in progress. Comparing `xmin` and `xmax` numerically with the current transaction ID is insufficient. PostgreSQL also consults transaction status; tuple hint bits can cache some conclusions about commit or abort status to reduce repeated status lookups. Hint bits do not replace snapshot visibility rules. [PGDG, 2024, Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/transaction-iso.html), [Transaction Status](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/transaction-status.html).

A version that is invisible to new snapshots may remain necessary to an existing snapshot. For example, transaction A establishes a Repeatable Read snapshot, then B updates a row and commits. New snapshots see B's version, but A can still require the predecessor. Removing that predecessor would violate A's snapshot semantics.

### Cleanup horizons: obsolete is not yet removable

Cleanup uses conservative visibility horizons derived from active transactions, snapshots, and other retention requirements. Conceptually, PostgreSQL must establish that no relevant observer can still require a tuple before reclaiming it. The implementation uses multiple horizons and relation-specific distinctions; there is no single global timestamp that fully explains every cleanup decision.

An old snapshot can consequently retain versions across many tables, including tables its owner has never queried. PostgreSQL does not normally track a complete per-snapshot inventory of every row that the transaction might later read. Conversely, an old snapshot does not prevent every cleanup operation: versions already obsolete before the relevant horizon may still be removable. [PGDG, 2024, Routine Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/routine-vacuuming.html).

Transaction age alone is an imperfect diagnosis:

- Read Committed normally obtains a fresh snapshot for each statement. A long active statement can retain history for its duration; the transaction does not normally retain one query snapshot across all statements.
- Repeatable Read and Serializable generally retain the transaction snapshot established by their first relevant statement. Merely executing `BEGIN` does not necessarily establish it.
- An open transaction that has acquired an XID can also constrain conservative cleanup horizons, even without a currently retained query snapshot. An idle Read Committed transaction that previously wrote data can therefore matter.
- An idle transaction with neither an assigned XID nor a retained snapshot does not pin cleanup merely because its `xact_start` is old.

These distinctions explain why both `backend_xid` and `backend_xmin` are useful when investigating retention. [PGDG, 2024, Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/transaction-iso.html), [Monitoring Statistics](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/monitoring-stats.html).

### What VACUUM reclaims—and what it cannot

Ordinary VACUUM removes reclaimable tuple versions, cleans index entries as needed, and makes space available for reuse within the relation. It also maintains visibility information and performs freezing. Opportunistic heap-page pruning, including cleanup of suitable HOT chains, can reclaim some storage between VACUUM runs. VACUUM is therefore essential maintenance, but is not the only cleanup mechanism. [PGDG, 2024, VACUUM](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/sql-vacuum.html), [HOT](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/storage-hot.html).

The visibility map tracks all-visible and all-frozen heap pages. All-visible pages can allow index-only scans to avoid heap visibility checks. All-frozen pages can be skipped by later freezing scans when appropriate. These bits summarize page properties; they do not make an otherwise unsafe tuple removable. [PGDG, 2024, Visibility Map](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/storage-vm.html).

Ordinary VACUUM generally leaves the table file at its existing size, with reusable space inside it. It can sometimes release completely empty trailing pages to the operating system. `VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table, needs additional disk space during the operation, and takes an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock. It is not routine background maintenance. [PGDG, 2024, Routine Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/routine-vacuuming.html).

Long-lived snapshots can cause successive UPDATE and DELETE operations to accumulate versions that cannot yet be removed. That increases storage demand and can increase scanning and maintenance work. Heap and index growth depend on workload, HOT eligibility, free space, and index structure. Retained versions are temporarily required history; after the blocker disappears, ordinary VACUUM can make their space reusable without necessarily shrinking the files. Ending a blocker enables cleanup but does not itself perform all cleanup.

### Autovacuum: scheduling cannot override visibility

Autovacuum schedules VACUUM and ANALYZE using table statistics and configurable thresholds. For PostgreSQL 17, the ordinary UPDATE/DELETE-driven vacuum trigger uses approximately:

`vacuum threshold = autovacuum_vacuum_threshold + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor × estimated table tuples`

The documented defaults are 50 tuples and a scale factor of 0.2. Thus, a table estimated to contain 1,000,000 tuples has a calculated trigger of 200,050 obsolete tuples. This is arithmetic from defaults, not a measurement or a guarantee about the exact execution time. Statistics estimates, launcher scheduling, available workers, locks, and table overrides affect when work actually starts. PostgreSQL also has an insertion-driven vacuum trigger, important for visibility-map maintenance and freezing on insert-heavy tables. [PGDG, 2024, Automatic Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/routine-vacuuming.html#AUTOVACUUM), [Autovacuum Configuration](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/runtime-config-autovacuum.html).

Per-table thresholds can be preferable to relying on one scale factor for every table. Autovacuum cost limits and delays throttle maintenance I/O; worker availability and competing work also constrain progress. Lower thresholds or more maintenance capacity can help when vacuum starts too late or cannot keep up. They cannot authorize removal of versions still required by an old horizon. A vacuum that reports many tuples dead but not yet removable calls for investigating retention, rather than simply repeating the same vacuum.

Autovacuum can normally operate alongside ordinary reads and writes, but conflicting locks can delay it. Anti-wraparound autovacuum has special treatment and can be launched even when ordinary autovacuum is disabled. Temporary tables require maintenance by their owning session because autovacuum cannot access them. [PGDG, 2024, Routine Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/routine-vacuuming.html).

### Freezing and XID wraparound

Normal transaction IDs are 32-bit, and ordering uses wraparound-aware comparisons. The safe ordering window is approximately half the XID space, about 2 billion transactions. This is transaction consumption, not elapsed wall-clock time: an idle cluster and a transaction-heavy cluster age differently.

PostgreSQL freezes sufficiently old committed tuple insertion XIDs so those tuples remain understood as predating normal snapshots after XID wraparound. In modern PostgreSQL, freezing is represented using tuple flags; the original `xmin` value can remain physically present. Describing every freeze as replacing the field with `FrozenTransactionId` is therefore inaccurate. [PGDG, 2024, Preventing Transaction ID Wraparound Failures](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/routine-vacuuming.html#VACUUM-FOR-WRAPAROUND).

PostgreSQL 17 documents these defaults:

- `vacuum_freeze_min_age`: 50 million transactions, controlling when tuple XIDs become candidates for freezing.
- `vacuum_freeze_table_age`: 150 million transactions, influencing when VACUUM performs an aggressive scan to advance freezing coverage.
- `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`: 200 million transactions, triggering protective autovacuum based on table XID age.

These are different controls, not three names for one deadline. The protective autovacuum trigger is deliberately far below the wraparound danger boundary. Aggressive vacuum can skip pages already known to be all-frozen. PostgreSQL also has a vacuum failsafe that prioritizes wraparound protection, including bypassing cost delays and some nonessential work when necessary. These mechanisms cannot override a transaction that still makes a proposed freeze unsafe. [PGDG, 2024, Vacuum Configuration](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/runtime-config-client.html#RUNTIME-CONFIG-CLIENT-STATEMENT), [Autovacuum Configuration](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/runtime-config-autovacuum.html).

Long-running transactions can constrain how far freezing may safely advance. However, retained dead tuples and freezing are distinct problems: an old snapshot does not prevent freezing every tuple. Sufficiently old committed insertions can still be frozen when safely before the relevant cutoff. `relfrozenxid` and `datfrozenxid` summarize freezing progress at table and database levels; their ages are conservative maintenance indicators, not exact counts of unfrozen rows.

If freezing cannot advance sufficiently, PostgreSQL warns and eventually refuses new XID assignment before unsafe wraparound occurs. Increasing freeze-age settings or disabling routine autovacuum does not resolve an ancient transaction or retention blocker. MultiXact IDs have separate aging and maintenance requirements. [PGDG, 2024, Routine Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/routine-vacuuming.html).

### Other holders of history and practical diagnosis

A client transaction is not the only possible blocker. Prepared transactions, replication-slot `xmin`, slot `catalog_xmin` for catalog retention, and standby feedback can constrain cleanup. A replication slot retaining WAL through `restart_lsn` is a related but distinct storage issue; retained WAL is not itself proof that heap tuples are pinned. Standby feedback trades fewer recovery conflicts for potentially greater retention on the primary. [PGDG, 2024, Replication Slots](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/view-pg-replication-slots.html), [Standby Configuration](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/runtime-config-replication.html#RUNTIME-CONFIG-REPLICATION-STANDBY).

Useful evidence includes `pg_stat_activity` transaction state, `xact_start`, `backend_xid`, and `backend_xmin`; `pg_prepared_xacts`; replication-slot horizons; estimated `n_dead_tup` and vacuum history in `pg_stat_user_tables`; `VACUUM VERBOSE` output; and `age(relfrozenxid)` and `age(datfrozenxid)`. Estimated dead-tuple counts are not exact measurements of reclaimable bytes or physical bloat.

Operationally, distinguish retention blockers from insufficient vacuum capacity. Close or appropriately cancel abandoned transactions, bound snapshot duration where application semantics permit, maintain replication consumers, and then allow vacuum to reclaim eligible space. Session timeouts such as `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` can prevent some abandoned transactions, but do not address every long query or replication horizon. Determine whether the resulting free space will be reused before choosing a disruptive rewrite solely to reduce file size.
